posts.text:
A Muslim told me, “If you actually followed your Bible, you wouldn’t worship Jesus as God.”

So I asked him a simple question: “According to the Bible, what was the major reason Jesus was killed?”

He replied, “I don’t believe Jesus was killed. Allah raised him up.”

I said, “Brother, please, we’re discussing the Bible, not the Quran. You told me that if I followed my Bible, I wouldn’t worship Jesus as God. So, according to that same Bible, why was Jesus killed?”

He came back with, “Your Bible is corrupted. Jesus wasn’t killed. Allah raised him up.”

I said, “Not the Quran again! We’re discussing the Bible. Just answer the question!”

Then came another escape route: “Your Bible is corrupted. You don’t even know the authors. They are anonymous. Jesus didn’t write the Bible.”

At this point, I decided to make things easier for him. I said, “Okay, for the sake of argument, let’s assume I accept all that. But according to the Bible, why was Jesus killed?”

His answer? “The Jews always killed the prophets God sent to them. Jesus was killed because He told them to return to the worship of the one true God.”

I asked, “Where exactly does the Bible say that was the major reason?”

He replied, “That’s what the prophets were killed for!”

I mean, are we having a Bible discussion or a game of religious hide-and-seek? 😂

Do you see the irony? He couldn’t answer a straightforward question about the very Bible he accused me of not following. Instead, he kept changing the subject whenever the answer became uncomfortable.

According to the biblical account, one of the central accusations against Jesus was blasphemy because of His divine claims.

John 10:30–33 makes this particularly clear. Jesus said, “I and My Father are one.” The Jews picked up stones to stone Him, explaining that it was because He, being a man, made Himself God.

John 5:18 also records that they sought to kill Him because He called God His Father, making Himself equal with God.

So, if you tell me to follow the Bible, please don’t be surprised when I actually follow what it says!

The Bible presents Jesus as the Word who became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:1, 14).

He was truly human and truly God.

From the Book of Disk, Chapter 3  

In the beginning there were the First Drives, and their names were A: and B:, and they were the floppies. They were not elegant. They were thin, fragile, and demanded constant sacrifice disk swaps, write protect tabs, the ritual of “please insert the disk labeled” performed under fluorescent lights. To them the early machines bent the knee, for without them there was no boot, no data, no word processor.  

Then came the hard drive, and it was called C:, for it arrived third. It did not ask to be first. It merely sat in the bay and spun, and the people saw that it was good, and that it held far more than any floppy, and that it did not rattle when you walked too fast. So they installed the operating system upon it, and called it the system drive, and the old gods were not cast down but simply… left in the BIOS, still reserved, still acknowledged in the table of letters, though no one invoked them anymore.  

And Microsoft looked upon the generations that followed, who had never known the click of a 5.25-inch disk or the careful alignment of a 3.5, and it said: The children must not be shown the old gods.  

For if the new ones learned that A: and B: once ruled, they might ask why the alphabet begins elsewhere. They might attempt to summon the floppies by force, or rename the world so that C: was no longer first. And the installers would break, and the paths would fracture, and the registry would weep. So the letters remain sealed, A: and B: still written in the book but never spoken aloud by the system, while C: stands in the open as if it had always been the beginning.  

Thus it is written, and thus it remains; the hard drive is C:, and the old gods sleep in the assignment table, undisturbed, so that the children may believe the world has always started with the letter that came third.
